field_rule: Switchgrass: compare the complete panicle, mature spikelets, collar and connected scaly rhizomes. Inspect blade-base hairs separately from the inner ligule. Regional sources differ on ligule terminology and node hairs; neither a hair-fringe appearance nor a hairy node alone rules it out. Usually the panicle is an open airy cloud, but an older USDA regional key explicitly includes contracted examples. Retain a genuinely long contracted panicle as a provisional switchgrass possibility, NOT proof: compare attached rhizomes, collar and spikelets and do not generalize the shape to all populations.

field_rule: Knotgrass combines wet-ground creeping stolons with usually paired (rarely three) unilateral flowering racemes. Bahia grass can produce two racemes but differs in low turf/rhizome architecture and spikelet structure. Thin paspalum may form just one or a few flowering branches but has different leafy habit and varietal hair traits; Florida paspalum forms robust upright bunches and bigger oval spikelets. In the less-common 3–4-raceme form described by the regional Flora, a knotgrass head may also satisfy the broad 'fingers clustered near the tip' button. Keep `paired_spikes` for the usual two, and `one_sided` for the arrangement of spikelets along each flattened raceme. Only permit `fingers` when three or four actual terminal racemes are seen, not when a pair merely looks forked. Confirm creeping rooted culms and mostly solitary spikelets against Bahia grass and other Paspalum species.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1306; FNA Paspalum distichum and UT Austin Williamson County species account
head.reference: The regional Diggs flora says 2 terminal one-sided branches, OCCASIONALLY 3–4, 2–6 cm long. UT Austin describes (1–)2(–3) spikelike branches paired or short-staggered near the end of the culm. Kew GrassBase typically gives 2(–3) paired unilateral racemes. The UI generic `fingers` means several narrow branches arising together NEAR the tip, so its 3–4-raceme variant is a legitimate conditional visual state. This does not imply most heads have 3–4 or that any 2-branch V is to be counted as 'several'. Preserve precise paired-Spikes and broad one-sided states.
reported_states: uncommon 3–4 closely grouped terminal racemes, fingerlike outline

field_rule: Actual archived Bob Harms whole flowering-specimen panel 1 shows several attached leafy shoots and panicles; panel 2 displays the entire dense short-branched seedhead; panel 3 magnifies overlapping glumes. A contracted ovoid to cylindrical head is a first clue (FNA 0.5–8 cm long, often 0.8–2 cm wide), but several introduced Phalaris look similar. The one- vs two-STERILE-LEMMA difference cannot be determined from head silhouette alone. Keep a LONG, NARROW contracted flowering head as a conditional Carolina canarygrass possibility: the 1999 regional Flora explicitly documents some individuals with elongated cylindrical heads to 12 cm. Most heads are shorter, compact oval cylinders. Confirm the true branched panicle and inspect lateral glume-vein spicules (usually 5 or fewer) and glume/spikelet dimensions before deciding between Carolina and narrow canarygrass; do NOT relabel the panicle a true unbranched spike.

field_rule: Use visible macro morphology first and defer difficult perennial-species separations to mature material, reliable grain tests and microscope when necessary. The regional vegetative account allows small clumps, solitary plants, and elongate scaly RHIZOMES that may also be absent. Keep tuft and true underground-rhizome observations eligible; neither alone distinguishes this plant from hidden dropseed.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses
broad_group_note: Existing Hays Botany description screened; historical flora treats Sporobolus compositus in infraspecific aggregates that do not directly map to all modern accepted species. Retain provisional head/habit states and flag taxon crosswalk.

head.reference: Vertical narrow panicle often partly enclosed by subtending upper sheath; contracted spike-like appearance, not a true single spike.

ligule.reference: Tiny CILIATE MEMBRANOUS ligule; hair fringe and membrane both permitted as broad photographic appearances. Taxon complexes/varieties still unresolved.

pericarp.source: UT Austin Plant Resources Center, Bob Harms, Texas Sporobolus complexes
pericarp.reference: Many modern keys use gelatinizing/swelling pericarp when wet vs non-gelatinizing in S. clandestinus. UT explains ambiguity of wet/moist/loose terms; requires multiple grains and lemma pubescence, not binary photograph based choice.

habit.source: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), Grasses of the Texas Hill Country, printed p. 64, Sporobolus compositus
habit.reference: Perennial specimens may be solitary or small-clumped; rhizomes are elongate and scaly OR absent, while stolons are absent. Retain broad tuft and underground-rhizome observations without imposing rhizome presence on every specimen. The authors find no dependable vegetative separation from S. clandestinus; mature lemmas and authenticated vouchers remain essential.
reported_states: elongate scaly rhizomes present or absent
habit.photo_voucher_support: No newly authenticated source or local specimen image verified for rhizome visibility. Taxonomic complex and grain/pericarp uncertainty retained.

diagnostic_checks.look: Look for the partly SHEATHED tall contracted panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: Tall/composite dropseed is usually a tufted perennial with narrow contracted flowering panicles ~5–26 cm, often partly hidden by the subtending leaf sheath. The ligule is a very short ciliate membrane/hair-fringe at field scale.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Poverty dropseed is an annual with much shorter 1–4 cm terminal AND axillary often sheathed panicles; S. clandestinus also forms narrow enclosed perennial heads.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA/Iowa grass account and UT Texas complex; sheath photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Iowa State — Sporobolus compositus

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine LEMMA surface rather than assuming all rough dropseed names agree
diagnostic_checks.check: The S. compositus complex is often diagnosed by relatively smooth, GLABROUS mature fertile lemma vs the visibly pubescent/scabrous opaque lemma of S. clandestinus. Typical S. compositus 4.5–5.4 mm single-floret spikelets and lemmas ~4.4–5.2 mm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: S. clandestinus typical 5–7 mm spikelets with pubescent 4–5 mm lemmas. Variation and both current/older names exist; compare actual same-scale spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Iowa State and UT Bob Harms; species-complex and variety interpretations not interchangeable
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Austin Plant Resources Center — Sporobolus compositus complex

diagnostic_checks.look: Be cautious with the moist pericarp test
diagnostic_checks.check: Pericarp of S. compositus is generally reported swelling/gelatinizing on soaking, whereas S. clandestinus stays loose but not gelatinous. UT Harms documents disagreement and ambiguity about interpreting 'loose', 'moist', and 'wet': a single uncertain drop does not confirm an identification.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Never perform a destructive wet seed test on the only voucher; record several grains and microscope lemma surface first.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: UT Texas detailed critique of pericarp key vs FNA/Riggins; source-qualified evidence, not pass/fail filter
diagnostic_checks.source: UT Plant Resources Center — Sporobolus pericarp caveats

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect a connected dropseed base for a scaly rhizome
diagnostic_checks.check: Some composite dropseeds have an elongate underground scaly rhizome; other plants lack it. A genuinely observed rhizome must not eliminate this species, but absence is not itself confirmation.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hidden dropseed (S. clandestinus) remains vegetatively inseparable by this treatment; check mature lemma pubescence and several connected spikelets before a species-level determination.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Direct regional vegetative-source account; connected local specimen and reproductive confirmation pending.
diagnostic_checks.source: Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015), p. 64

field_rule: Tripsacum genus clue = thick SAME spike with male region ABOVE and enlarged female beadlike lower joints BELOW. For exact species, verify a mature specimen; lookalike silhouettes and leaf width alone do not prove it. The same reproductive organ can also satisfy the broader 'long upright spike' picture when a single unbranched spike-like rame is present, or the 'fingers near the tip' choice when two or more thick terminal rames arise together. Regional descriptions report solitary and 2–3-branched heads, including Texas single-spike plants; confirm male-over-female sections before final ID.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1332; UT Austin PRC Tripsacum dactyloides; Kew GrassBase
head.reference: Diggs describes lower pistillate rachis and unbranched or 2–3 branched upper staminate region. UT Austin locally describes terminal spikes as solitary or two-branched in its Texas range. Kew GrassBase describes 1–10 single, paired, or digitate racemes (12–25 cm). In the broad visual filter, an individual thick single axis is `spike`; clustered 2–3 digitately arranged terminal branches meet `fingers`. Keep `mixed_gender` as the uniquely diagnostic appearance (hard lower female bead joints + upper male spikelets). Heads can be damaged or partly abscised; no choice alone proves species.

two to several near-terminal digitate branches

diagnostic_checks.look: Separate the male upper section from female lower section
diagnostic_checks.check: On a single spike-like branch, the delicate upper staminate portion bears paired male spikelets, while below it the thick female rachis holds embedded pistillate spikelets in hard beadlike segments.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Sorghum and Sorghastrum also have sex-differentiated spikelets but not this hard, recessed lower female section
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; matched head at flowering/fruiting needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the female rachis joint and inner collar
diagnostic_checks.check: Female units have a thick, excavated, jointed rachis with craterlike attachment; the segments ultimately separate. Existing flora describes an inner membrane ligule fringed by hairs; do not confuse it with mature female rachis hairs.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Other Tripsacum species and maize relatives require segment/rachis measurements and full specimen authentication
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase-backed; species-level comparison still pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew POWO / GrassBase — Tripsacum dactyloides

diagnostic_checks.look: Count the distinct spike-like axes in eastern gamagrass
diagnostic_checks.check: Look for a single thick terminal spike-like branch OR a cluster of 2–3 (sometimes more) palmately arranged branches. The former matches the generic spike icon; the latter can resemble short stout fingers near the tip. On either form, identify the female hard lower beads and paired male upper spikelets before treating it as gamagrass.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Generic spike and fingers icons are shared with other grasses. Do not use either alone to separate Tripsacum from Elymus, Eleusine or Chloris; species-level female rachis and male-spikelet structure are decisive.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Diggs, UT Austin species morphology and Kew GrassBase agree on variable branch count; connected Hays sex-zone photo and voucher pending.

field_rule: Rank photos by what they truly show: flowering branch/shape first, followed by mature spikelet length and lower glume measured under 10–20×. Do not treat unmeasured photogenic heads as proof of native versus introduced species. Mature Texas signalgrass heads can have seven or more closely appressed unilateral racemes along a central axis; selecting the seven-plus one-sided option must retain it. The count is conditional, not universal (Kew describes 3–10). Confirm the long 5–6 mm spikelets and strongly veined lower glume with a lens before final identification.
trait_provenance: Existing Hays Botany Poaceae species card morphology; preliminary multi-access character states; needs field QA

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, Urochloa texana account; Kew GrassBase / POWO, Urochloa texana
head.reference: Diggs describes a compact terminal panicle of erect-appressed branches. Kew GrassBase specifies 3–10 unilateral racemes borne along 7–18 cm central axis. Thus a mature head with >=7 unilateral branches legitimately qualifies for the seven-plus one-sided UI choice. Preserve original general one_sided option for heads with fewer branches. Do not mistake a robust count for species-level confirmation; use lower glume (~2/3 length; 5–7 nerves) and measured spikelets.
reported_states: 7–10 unilateral branches occasionally on mature heads
head.photo_voucher_support: No Hays connected original whole head with reliably counted racemes and same-plant spikelet dissection newly validated.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt, PDF p. 259
habit.reference: Annual that may creep and root from lower nodes; not always an upright tuft.

ligule.source: Kew GrassBase under Brachiaria texana; UT Austin regional morphology
ligule.reference: True ligule is a ciliate MEMBRANE, ~1–1.5 mm (UT Austin 1–1.8 mm). Hairlike cilia conceal the membrane base; retain hair and membrane broad visual states, not absence.

diagnostic_checks.look: Open the true collar beneath the hair fringe
diagnostic_checks.check: Texas signalgrass has a ciliate MEMBRANE 1–1.5 mm, often appearing like pure hairs until magnified. Regional UT Austin material describes a 1–1.8 mm fused membrane at the blade–sheath joint.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum usually has a more evident plain papery ligule; collar shape alone is genus-level.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase / UT Texas morphology; retain both broad visual states pending actual photo
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Urochloa texana under Brachiaria

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure spikelet and LOWER glume
diagnostic_checks.check: Published spikelets around 5–6 mm, paired along unilateral erect-appressed branches. The developed lower glume is around TWO-THIRDS the spikelet, usually 5–7 veined. The upper glume is about full spikelet length.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum mostly has no lower glume; Brownseed signalgrass has smaller 2.4–3 mm spikelets and a much shorter lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew source checked; mature same-plant dissection needed
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Urochloa texana

diagnostic_checks.look: Look at the textured upper fertile lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: The hard upper fertile lemma is usually 3.5–4 mm, finely wrinkled across its back. Plants may be upright or sprawl and root at low nodes. Verify the annual growth base as well as a complete head.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Other Urochloa species also have wrinkled fertile lemmas: combine with the large spikelet and lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase checked; local specimen and photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Kew GrassBase — Urochloa texana

diagnostic_checks.look: Count the ascending one-sided Texas signalgrass branches
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew GrassBase documents 3–10 branches along the upper axis. Seven or more is a real but not required species state; preserve the broad one-sided option for 3–6-branch heads. Do not confuse the branches themselves with spikelets, which sit in pairs along their axes.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Brownseed signalgrass and other Urochloa species may share the head. Measure the larger 5–6 mm spikelets and strongly 5–7-veined, roughly two-thirds-length lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Diggs and Kew morphology reviewed; no new specimen/image/licensing signoff.
diagnostic_checks.source: Diggs et al. (1999), Urochloa texana; Kew GrassBase — Urochloa texana
